briefs.body:
# Competitive field

## Overview

Capital One's own 10-K filings describe a competitive field spanning three lines of business — credit cards, consumer/commercial banking, and direct (online) banking — plus a payments ecosystem increasingly contested by non-bank entrants. The packet's most consistent framing, repeated near-verbatim across FY2015–FY2019 filings, is that "each of our business segments operates in a highly competitive environment, and we face competition in all aspects of our business from numerous bank and non-bank providers of financial services" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM1]. No market-share, deposit-ranking, or revenue figures for named competitors appear anywhere in the packet; all competitive claims below are qualitative.

## Credit Card Segment

Across FY2016, FY2017, and FY2019 filings, Capital One states that its "Credit Card business competes with international, national, regional and local issuers of Visa and MasterCard credit cards, as well as with American Express®, Discover Card®, private-label card brands, and, to a certain extent, issuers of debit cards" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2017-02-23_0000927628-17-000115#main:ITEM1] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM1] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2020-02-20_0000927628-20-000102#main:ITEM1]. The stated basis of competition is consistent across years: "customers are attracted to credit card issuers largely on the basis of price, credit limit, reward programs and other product features" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2017-02-23_0000927628-17-000115#main:ITEM1]. By FY2020, Capital One's risk factors add that "competition for rewards customers may result in higher rewards expenses, or we may fail to attract new customers or retain existing rewards customers due to increasing competition for these consumers" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1A] — the first packet instance of a cost-side framing (rewards expense) rather than pure feature competition.

## Consumer and Commercial Banking

Capital One describes its Consumer Banking and Commercial Banking businesses as competing "with national, state and direct banks for deposits, commercial and auto loans, mortgages and trust accounts, as well as with savings and loan associations and credit unions for loans and deposits," with additional competition from "automotive finance companies, mortgage banking companies and other financial services providers" and from "non-depository institutions" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM1] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2017-02-23_0000927628-17-000115#main:ITEM1]. The filings flag a structural risk: "securities firms and insurance companies that elect to become financial holding companies may acquire banks and other financial institutions," and such combinations "could significantly change the competitive environment" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM1]. Technology is named as a second structural pressure — "technological advances enable more companies to provide financial services" and "may diminish the importance of depository institutions and other financial intermediaries in the transfer of funds between parties" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM1].

## Direct Banking

Capital One's self-description as a scale leader in online banking is explicit and recurs across the packet's date range: as of December 31, 2015, the company states it "operate[d] the largest online direct banking institution in the U.S. by deposits" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM1A]; by December 31, 2020, the language softens to "one of the largest online direct banks in the United States by deposits" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1A] — a shift the packet does not explain (no intervening filing clarifies whether this reflects a ranking change, a legal/wording revision, or growth by rivals). Both filings describe "aggressive pricing throughout the industry" as a threat to deposit retention and acquisition cost, and note that direct-banking customers can shift balances "rapidly" due to the flexibility and "financial and technological sophistication" of the online customer base [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM1A] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1A]. The FY2020 filing adds a scale-disadvantage risk absent from FY2015 language: "some of our competitors are substantially larger than we are," with advantages in "a more diversified product and customer base... operational efficiencies, broad-based local distribution capabilities, lower-cost funding and larger existing branch networks" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1A].

## Payments and Fintech Competition

The FY2015 risk factors describe the "global payments industry" as "highly competitive and... rapidly changing and increasingly subject to regulatory scrutiny," naming competition from "aggregators and web-based and wireless payment platforms or technologies, digital currencies, prepaid systems and payment services" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM1A]. By FY2023, Capital One's Item 1 explicitly folds fintech into its competitor set: "we also consider new and emerging companies in digital and mobile payments and other financial technology providers among our competitors. We compete with many forms of payment mechanisms, systems and products, offered by both bank and non-bank providers" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1]. The stated basis of competition broadens accordingly to "quality and range of... products and services, transaction execution, innovation and price," with success also contingent on "ability to keep pace with innovation, in particular in the development of new technology platforms" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1].

## Cross-Issuer Context: Discover's Network Position

Discover's own 10-Ks (FY2015–FY2020) name Capital One (360) as a direct-banking peer: Discover states it has "acquisition and servicing capabilities similar to other large direct banks, including Ally, American Express, Barclays, Capital One (360), Goldm[an...]" [src:edgar-dfs/10-K_2020-02-26_0001393612-20-000009#main:PARTI] [src:edgar-dfs/10-K_2021-02-17_0001393612-21-000014#main:PARTI]. This confirms, from a competitor's own disclosure, that Capital One 360 is treated as a comparable direct-deposit franchise. Discover's filings otherwise describe network-level competition (Visa, MasterCard, American Express, PULSE vs. Interlink/Maestro/STAR) that is adjacent to but distinct from Capital One's card-issuer competition [src:edgar-dfs/10-K_2018-02-21_0001393612-18-000012#main:PARTI].

## Gaps

The Events list consists almost entirely of 8-K filings dated 2025–2026, nearly all tagged "(other)" or "Substantive Content Not Provided" with no extracted text, plus single instances tagged "(results)" and "(capital_action)" [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2026-04-21_0000927628-26-000039] [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2026-04-07_0001193125-26-145764]. None of these carry competitive-field content in the packet as provided, so no post-2024 competitive developments (market-share shifts, new entrants, M&A, fintech partnerships) can be asserted. The packet also contains no quantitative market-share, deposit-ranking, or revenue-comparison data for any named competitor, and no direct discussion of the Discover acquisition's effect on Capital One's competitive position — a notable omission given Discover appears throughout as both a named card-network competitor and, via its own filings, a direct-banking peer.

briefs.body:
# Corporate history and lineage

## Corporate history and lineage

### Corporate form and founding
Capital One Financial Corporation is a Delaware corporation established in 1994, headquartered in McLean, Virginia [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM1]. This founding date and jurisdiction are repeated consistently across filings through the most recent 10-K on file, including FY2022 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM1], FY2023 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1], FY2024 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM1], and FY2025 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1]. The packet contains no filing describing the pre-1994 formation, spin-off from Signet Banking Corporation, or IPO — only the incorporation year and the residue of that lineage in later governance documents (see below).

### The Signet Banking Corporation reference and its 2023 removal
The one explicit textual trace of Capital One's pre-1994 lineage in this packet is a set of references to "Signet Banking Corporation" embedded in the company's Restated Certificate of Incorporation. In 2023, Capital One's board and shareholders acted to strip these references out. The 2023 proxy statement asked shareholders to approve "amendments to Capital One Financial Corporation's Restated Certificate of Incorporation to remove remaining supermajority voting requirements and references to Signet Banking Corporation" [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM1] [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:preamble]. The board unanimously recommended a "FOR" vote on this item [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM2], and the proxy card itself listed it as management item 2 [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6]. The subsequent 8-K confirms shareholders approved the amendment at the May 4, 2023 annual meeting, alongside ratification of Ernst & Young LLP as auditor and adoption of the Seventh Amended and Restated 2004 Stock Incentive Plan [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2023-05-09_0000927628-23-000197#main]. The packet does not include the certificate text itself or any narrative explaining what Signet Banking Corporation was or its relationship to Capital One's founding — only that references to it existed in the charter as of early 2023 and were formally excised. This is a governance-cleanup event, not a substantive account of lineage, and should be flagged as such in any downstream brief.

### The North Fork acquisition (2006) and its long tail
The most substantively documented acquisition in the packet is the December 2006 acquisition of North Fork Bancorporation, Inc. This transaction brought two problem units into Capital One that were run off over the following decade-plus as discontinued operations: GreenPoint Mortgage Funding, Inc.'s wholesale mortgage origination business, and the manufactured housing operations of GreenPoint Credit, LLC (a GreenPoint subsidiary) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2017-02-23_0000927628-17-000115#main:ITEM8]. The manufactured housing book had actually been sold to a third party in 2004, before North Fork owned it, but Capital One inherited retained interests and obligations in it through the acquisition [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2016-08-01_0000927628-16-000200#main:ITEM1]. The wholesale mortgage origination unit itself was closed in Q3 2007 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2016-11-03_0000927628-16-000228#main:ITEM1]. This discontinued-operations treatment persisted in quarterly and annual filings for over a decade: it appears in the Q1 2016 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2016-05-04_0000927628-16-000160#main:ITEM2], Q2 2016 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2016-08-01_0000927628-16-000200#main:ITEM1], Q3 2016 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2016-11-03_0000927628-16-000228#main:ITEM1], FY2016 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2017-02-23_0000927628-17-000115#main:ITEM8], and Q3 2018 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2018-11-01_0000927628-18-000317#main:ITEM1] reports. By Q3 2018, the residual size of this legacy was small: income from discontinued operations, net of tax, was $1 million in Q3 2018 versus a $30 million loss in Q3 2017, and $7 million versus $26 million loss for the nine months ended September 30 in 2018 vs. 2017, respectively; as of September 30, 2018, Capital One had "no significant continuing involvement" in the wholesale mortgage unit [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2018-11-01_0000927628-18-000317#main:ITEM1]. In Q4 2017, Capital One took on the obligation to exercise remaining clean-up calls on certain manufactured housing securitizations under an agreement with the third-party servicer [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2018-11-01_0000927628-18-000317#main:ITEM1]. The North Fork deal also generated PCI (purchased credit-impaired) loan accounting alongside later acquisitions (HFS in Q4 2015, ING Direct, Chevy Chase) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2017-02-23_0000927628-17-000115#main:ITEM7].

### Mortgage origination lineage: three acquired subsidiaries
The packet identifies a second, related lineage thread: Capital One's mortgage representation-and-warranty exposure traces to three acquired loan-originating subsidiaries — Capital One Home Loans, LLC (acquired February 2005), GreenPoint (acquired December 2006 via North Fork), and CCB (acquired February 2009, later merged into CONA) [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2016-05-04_0000927628-16-000160#main:ITEM2]. As of March 31, 2016, the aggregate representation-and-warranty reserve across all three entities was $613 million, up from $610 million at December 31, 2015 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2016-05-04_0000927628-16-000160#main:ITEM2]. This confirms CCB→CONA as a distinct historical merger separate from the North Fork/GreenPoint lineage, though the packet gives no further detail on the CCB acquisition itself.

### Bank subsidiary consolidation: COBNA into CONA (2022)
A more recent structural simplification is documented directly: on October 1, 2022, Capital One completed the "Bank Merger," merging Capital One Bank (USA), National Association (COBNA) into Capital One, National Association (CONA), with CONA surviving [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM1]. Prior to this, filings described two "principal subsidiaries" — COBNA (credit/debit cards, lending, deposits) and CONA (broad banking products) — collectively "the Banks" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2017-02-23_0000927628-17-000115#main:ITEM8 cites elsewhere; see 10-K_2018-02-21#ITEM1 and 10-K_2019-02-20#ITEM1]. Specifically, FY2017 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM1] and FY2018 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM1] 10-Ks both describe this two-bank structure. Post-merger, FY2022 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM1] and FY2023 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1] 10-Ks describe CONA as the sole "principal operating subsidiary," with "the Bank" redefined to mean CONA after the merger and CONA-and-COBNA collectively before it.

### The Discover merger (2025)
The packet documents a major, recent structural event: on May 18, 2025 (the "Closing Date"), Discover Financial Services merged into Capital One and Discover Bank merged into CONA [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1]. The FY2025 10-K frames this integration as coinciding with a repositioning of Capital One's business description, from a "diversified financial services holding company" to one operating "as a global payments provider and diversified financial institution" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1], and states Capital One became the largest credit card issuer in the U.S. by outstanding balance as of December 31, 2025 — up from third-largest as of FY2022–FY2024 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1] versus [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM1] and [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1]. The merger's registration mechanics (S-4, filed 2024-04-19) are represented in the packet only via boilerplate Securities Act liability/reoffering-prospectus undertakings (Item 22), with no deal terms, valuation, or timeline narrative included [src:edgar-cof/S-4_2024-04-19_0001193125-24-101304#main:ITEM22].

## Gaps

- **No pre-1994 lineage documented.** The packet does not explain what Signet Banking Corporation was, its relationship to Capital One's 1994 spin-off/founding, or why its name appeared in the charter — only that references to it were removed in 2023.
- **No S-4 deal narrative for the Discover merger.** The only S-4 excerpt in the packet is generic Item 22 undertakings; no merger consideration, exchange ratio, rationale, or regulatory approval history is present.
- **CCB acquisition undetailed.** CCB's February 2009 acquisition and 2009 merger into CONA is named once in passing; no filing in the packet describes the transaction itself.
- **No HFS, ING Direct, or Chevy Chase acquisition narrative.** These are named only as sources of PCI loans in a glossary entry, with no deal facts.
- **Numerical revenue series (FY2008–2026Q1) is present but not tied to any specific acquisition or divestiture in the narrative sources**, so it cannot be used here to quantify the financial impact of any named corporate event without speculation.

briefs.title: Credit cycle posture
briefs.body:
# Credit cycle posture

## Credit Cycle Posture

### Underwriting Philosophy and Governance

Capital One's stated credit doctrine is built on the assumption that loans will face conditions worse than those prevailing at origination. Unsecured consumer underwriting "generally assume[s] that loans will be subject to an environment in which losses are higher than those prevailing at the time of underwriting," while commercial underwriting requires "strong cash flow, collateral, covenants and guarantees" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM7]. Credit policy is organized around five standards — customer selection, underwriting, monitoring, remediation, and portfolio management — each backed by detailed procedures, with customer selection aimed at generating "above hurdle returns" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM7]. Governance runs through the Chief Risk Officer together with Chief Consumer and Chief Commercial Credit Officers, who hold formal approval authority for credit decisions, with Division Presidents responsible for managing credit risk within their segments [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM7]. By FY2025, auto underwriting is described concretely as FICO-, LTV-, and credit-bureau-driven, and commercial underwriting continues to rely on borrower financial condition, industry assessment, collateral/guarantee evaluation, and an assigned risk rating with a monitoring schedule [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM7].

### Pre-Pandemic Cycle: 2015–2019

Credit metrics through the mid-cycle years show gradual normalization punctuated by idiosyncratic portfolio stress rather than broad deterioration. In FY2015, the net charge-off (NCO) rate rose 3 bps to 1.75% and 30+ day delinquency rose 9 bps to 3.00%, driven by taxi medallion and oil-and-gas exposure in Commercial Banking; the allowance for loan and lease losses grew $747 million to $5.1 billion, with coverage up 13 bps to 2.23% [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM7]. Consumer Banking's NCO rate ticked up 7 bps to 0.83% in Q2 2016 as auto loans grew as a share of the portfolio, even as 30+ day delinquency fell 60 bps to 4.07% [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2016-08-01_0000927628-16-000200#main:ITEM2]. Going into 2018, management expected Domestic Card charge-off pressure from loan seasoning to moderate while auto finance charge-offs were expected to rise gradually [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7]. That played out in Q2 2018: NCO rate fell 25 bps to 2.42% against an elevated 2017 comparison base (oil-and-gas, taxi medallion), delinquency fell 43 bps to 3.05%, and the allowance declined $134 million to $7.4 billion as coverage rose to 3.12% [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2018-07-27_0000927628-18-000281#main:ITEM2]. Quarterly provision for credit losses stayed in a roughly $1.1–2.0 billion band from 2015 through 2019 [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts], consistent with a benign, seasoning-driven cycle rather than a systemic credit event.

### COVID-19 Shock and CECL Transition

The pandemic produced the sharpest discontinuity in the packet. Q1 2020 CECL adoption combined with pandemic-driven allowance builds to double the coverage ratio to 5.4% from 2.7% at year-end 2019, driving a $1.3 billion net loss [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2020-05-01_0000927628-20-000173#main:ITEM2]; the allowance itself rose $6.9 billion to $14.1 billion in the quarter [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2020-05-01_0000927628-20-000173#main:ITEM1]. Builds continued into Q2 2020, taking the allowance to $16.8 billion (+$9.6 billion since year-end 2019) [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2020-08-06_0000927628-20-000242#main:ITEM1]. For full-year 2020, the company booked $5.0 billion in allowance builds across Q1–Q2 on expectations of economic worsening, ending the year with net income of $2.7 billion and a coverage ratio of 6.19%, up from 2.71% at year-end 2019 — the allowance itself rose $8.4 billion to $15.6 billion, reflecting both CECL adoption and pandemic-related builds [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1][src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. Quarterly provision spiked to $5.4 billion in 2020Q1 alone, versus a pre-pandemic quarterly norm near $1.3–1.7 billion [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts]. The reversal came fast: by Q1 2021, government stimulus and strong credit performance cut the NCO rate 151 bps year-over-year to 1.21% and delinquency 63 bps to 1.98%, allowing the allowance to release $1.5 billion to $14.0 billion (coverage down 42 bps to 5.77%) [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2021-05-07_0000927628-21-000175#main:ITEM2]. Full-year 2021 NCO reached a historically low 0.88% [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6].

### Post-Pandemic Normalization: 2022–2024

From 2022 onward, the packet documents a sustained, multi-year normalization cycle rather than a shock. FY2022 NCO rose to 1.36% (Domestic Card 2.5%), with provision swinging from a $1.9 billion benefit in 2021 to a $5.8 billion charge, alongside CET1 of 12.5% [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6]. Q1 2023 continued this trend: NCO rose 110 bps year-over-year to 2.21% on "continued credit normalization," while the allowance grew $1.1 billion to $14.3 billion (coverage +40 bps to 4.64%) [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2023-05-05_0000927628-23-000168#main:ITEM2]. FY2023 NCO reached 2.7% (Domestic Card 4.6%), provision rose to $10.4 billion, and CET1 stood at 12.9% [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2024-03-20_0001193125-24-072711#main:ITEM4]. FY2024 NCO climbed further to 3.4% (Domestic Card 5.9%), provision to $11.7 billion, and CET1 to 13.5% [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2025-03-27_0001193125-25-065530#main:ITEM4]. XBRL allowance balances corroborate a steady build across this window, from $11.3 billion (2022-03-31) to $16.3 billion (2024-12-31) [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts].

### Allowance Step-Change in 2025

XBRL data show the allowance for credit losses jumping from $15.9 billion (2025-03-31) to $23.9 billion (2025-06-30), then holding near $23.1–23.6 billion through 2026-03-31 [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts]. This is a structural break in the series — roughly 50% larger than any prior quarter-end balance in the packet — but no MD&A, 10-K, or proxy excerpt in this packet explains the driver. It must be flagged, not interpreted.

### Liquidity Framework as Credit-Cycle Complement

Capital One frames liquidity risk as a companion discipline to credit risk: the Liquidity Adequacy Framework uses internal and regulatory stress testing to keep the balance sheet "resilient to uncertainties" from systemic or idiosyncratic events, backed by a Contingency Funding Plan and Recovery Plan [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM7]. CECL-era allowance mechanics extend to off-balance-sheet exposure: unfunded lending commitments in Commercial Banking are reserved using the same measurement objectives as funded loans, with builds/releases running through the provision line [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. Partnership credit card arrangements further shape reported losses, since expected partner reimbursements are netted against the allowance and reduce reported net charge-offs and provision [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM8].

## Gaps

- **2025 allowance jump unexplained**: the $8B step-up in allowance between 2025-03-31 and 2025-06-30 [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts] has no corresponding narrative source in this packet (no 10-Q/10-K MD&A excerpt covering that period is included). Cause, portfolio mix, and coverage-ratio impact cannot be stated.
- **No FY2025 charge-off/delinquency rate or coverage ratio**: the packet's narrative credit-performance disclosures stop at FY2024 (DEF14A filed 2025-03-27); the FY2025 10-K excerpt provided covers only underwriting methodology, not realized credit metrics [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM7].
- **2025–2026 8-K events are stubs**: all listed 8-Ks from 2025-08-15 through 2026-08-17 are logged only as filing metadata ("other," "results," "capital_action") with no extracted substantive content, so no credit-cycle-relevant disclosures (e.g., earnings commentary, capital actions) from this window can be cited.
- **No allowance coverage ratio for 2022–2024 quarter-ends**: dollar allowance balances are available via XBRL, but coverage-ratio percentages for these periods are only sourced at annual points via the proxy tables; intra-year coverage trends cannot be reconstructed precisely.
- **Cyber consent order items** (OCC order lifted 2022; FRB order lifted 2023) appear in the governance/risk tables alongside credit metrics but are operational-risk, not credit-cycle, disclosures; included only where the packet bundles them under "Risk management and compliance" [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6][src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2024-03-20_0001193125-24-072711#main:ITEM4].

briefs.title: The 2019 data breach and aftermath
briefs.body:
# The 2019 data breach and aftermath

## The 2019 data breach and aftermath

### The incident

On March 22–23, 2019, an outside individual exploited a configuration vulnerability to gain unauthorized access to Capital One's systems, obtaining personal information belonging to people who had applied for its credit card products and to existing credit card customers [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1]. Capital One did not disclose the breach publicly until July 29, 2019 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2025-11-03_0000927628-25-000276#main:ITEM1]. Management reported the event to the Board on July 19, 2019, ten days before public disclosure [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2020-03-19_0001193125-20-079122#main:ITEM5]. The company states it "immediately fixed the configuration vulnerability" and retained an outside cybersecurity firm that confirmed the fix, verifying no other instances existed in its environment [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2020-03-19_0001193125-20-079122#main:ITEM5] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1]. The individual responsible was arrested by the FBI on July 29, 2019, and federal prosecution followed; the U.S. Attorney's Office stated it believed the data had been recovered with no evidence of fraud or further sharing [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2020-03-19_0001193125-20-079122#main:ITEM5].

### Board and governance response

Following discovery, independent members of the Risk Committee, Audit Committee, Governance and Nominating Committee, and the full Board — including directors with cybersecurity and technology experience — met over 20 times to review the incident and the company's response, supplemented by informal update sessions with management [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2020-03-19_0001193125-20-079122#main:ITEM5]. The Board also engaged independent third-party experts for ongoing incident-response and root-cause reporting [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2020-03-19_0001193125-20-079122#main:ITEM5]. The packet does not provide detail beyond this summary on what governance or reporting-line changes resulted (see Gaps).

### Financial cost

Cumulative incremental expenses tied to remediation and response reached $138 million through year-end 2020, offset by $73 million in insurance recoveries; $66 million of that total was incurred during 2020 alone, offset by $39 million in insurance recoveries that year [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1]. These costs "mainly consist of customer notifications, credit monitoring, technology costs, and professional and legal support" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1]. Capital One carries cyber risk insurance with a $400 million coverage limit and a $10 million deductible, met in the third quarter of 2019 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1]. As of the FY2020 10-K, the company expected any further net expenses in future periods to be immaterial and stated it did not believe the incident would materially impact its strategy or long-term financial health [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1]. The packet contains no cost figures after FY2020 (see Gaps).

### Regulatory resolution

In August 2020, Capital One entered consent orders with the Federal Reserve and the OCC arising from regulatory reviews of the incident and tied to ongoing cybersecurity and operational risk management enhancements [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. It paid an $80 million penalty to the U.S. Treasury under the OCC agreement; the Federal Reserve agreement carried no monetary penalty [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. The OCC terminated its consent order on August 31, 2022 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM1A] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2023-05-05_0000927628-23-000168#main:ITEM1]. The packet does not indicate whether the Federal Reserve order has since been lifted (see Gaps). Separately, the company received inquiries from Congress, federal regulators, relevant Canadian regulators, the Department of Justice, and roughly fourteen state Attorneys General regarding the incident, and stated it was cooperating with these offices [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8].

### Litigation

Consumer and securities litigation followed the disclosure. As of the Q1/Q2 2020 10-Qs, Capital One had been named in approximately 73 putative consumer class actions (61 in U.S. federal courts, 12 in Canadian courts), consolidated for pretrial proceedings before a multi-district litigation panel in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, Alexandria Division [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2020-05-01_0000927628-20-000173#main:ITEM1] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2020-08-06_0000927628-20-000242#main:ITEM1]. A parallel securities class action named the company and certain officers, alleging violations of federal securities laws tied to statements and omissions about information security practices, with a proposed class period of purchasers/acquirers of Capital One securities from July 23, 2015 to July 29, 2019 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8].

By mid-2025, the U.S. consumer and securities claims are no longer discussed in the packet's Cybersecurity Incident disclosures; only the Canadian track remains active. As of the Q2 and Q3 2025 10-Qs, Capital One is named in 4 putative consumer class actions in Canadian courts [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2025-07-31_0000927628-25-000247#main:ITEM1] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2025-11-03_0000927628-25-000276#main:ITEM1]. Procedurally: in Q2 2022 a British Columbia trial court preliminarily certified a class of impacted Canadian consumers excluding Quebec; that certification was appealed, and on July 4, 2024 the British Columbia Court of Appeal denied both parties' appeals [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2025-11-03_0000927628-25-000276#main:ITEM1]. In Q3 2023 a Quebec trial court preliminarily authorized a class of impacted Quebec consumers; on appeal, the Quebec Court of Appeal affirmed the trial court's ruling on February 25, 2025 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2025-11-03_0000927628-25-000276#main:ITEM1]. The remaining two Canadian actions, both pending in Alberta, remain at a preliminary stage [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2025-11-03_0000927628-25-000276#main:ITEM1]. The packet gives no outcome, dismissal, or settlement figure for the U.S. MDL consumer or securities cases, nor for the Canadian actions (see Gaps).

### Framing in current risk disclosure

Capital One's FY2021 and FY2022 10-Ks continue to cite the 2019 incident as a live risk-factor example, noting it "resulted in fines, litigation, government investigations and other regulatory enforcement inquiries, as well as consent orders" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2022-02-25_0000927628-22-000106#main:ITEM1A], with the FY2022 filing adding that consent orders were specifically with "the Federal Reserve and the OCC" and noting the OCC's August 2022 termination [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM1A]. A January 2025 Form 425 discusses an aggregate range of reasonably possible losses (up to $140 million as of June 30, 2024) for legal and regulatory matters generally, but does not attribute this figure specifically to the 2019 incident as opposed to other proceedings such as the card product misclassification matter [src:edgar-cof/425_2025-01-24_0001193125-25-011795#main].

## Gaps

- **Scale of exposure**: The packet gives no number for how many individuals' data was affected by the breach.
- **Costs after FY2020**: No cumulative or incremental expense/insurance-recovery figures are provided for 2021 onward; the FY2020 figure ($138M cumulative, $73M recovered) is the last such disclosure in the packet [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1].
- **Federal Reserve consent order status**: Only the OCC order's August 2022 termination is documented; the packet does not state whether or when the Federal Reserve order was lifted.
- **U.S. consumer/securities litigation outcomes**: The packet documents ~73 U.S./Canadian class actions and MDL consolidation as of mid-2020, and a securities class action, but contains no later update on settlement, dismissal, or resolution of the U.S. claims — only the Canadian track is tracked through 2025.
- **State AG inquiries and DOJ/Congressional inquiries**: No resolution, settlement, or closure is documented for the ~14 state AG inquiries or the Congressional/DOJ inquiries referenced in the FY2020 10-K [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8].
- **Technical root cause detail**: The packet describes a "configuration vulnerability" but provides no further technical detail on the exploit mechanism.

# Deposit strategy

## Deposit Strategy Doctrine Brief

## Funding Philosophy: Deposits as the Primary, Lower-Cost Source

Capital One's stated funding philosophy across multiple reporting periods is consistent: insured retail deposits are the primary funding source because they are relatively stable and lower-cost compared to alternatives. Wholesale funding — senior and subordinated notes, securitized debt obligations, federal funds purchased, repo agreements, and FHLB advances — is explicitly secondary and supplemental [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM7] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2024-08-01_0000927628-24-000264#main:ITEM2] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2024-10-31_0000927628-24-000306#main:ITEM2]. This framing is repeated verbatim across FY2023 and FY2024 10-Ks and two 2024 10-Qs, indicating it is a durable balance-sheet posture rather than a one-period statement.

The demand for that funding is tied to loan book growth, particularly credit cards: loans held for investment rose $8.1B to $320.5B in FY2023 and $7.3B to $327.8B in FY2024, both attributed primarily to credit card loan growth [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM7] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7]. Interim 2024 quarters show loans held roughly flat to slightly down ($320.2B at 9/30/2024, $318.2B at 6/30/2024) as commercial paydowns offset card and auto growth [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2024-10-31_0000927628-24-000306#main:ITEM2] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2024-08-01_0000927628-24-000264#main:ITEM2].

## The Discover Acquisition as a Deposit-Scale Event

Deposit strategy is inseparable from the Discover transaction. Pre-close investor materials from February–March 2024 framed Discover's direct-to-consumer deposit base as "$84 billion in stable, largely insured consumer deposits, the most sought-after funding source in banking" [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-040125#main] [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-03-06_0000927628-24-000114#main]. The deal was also pitched as a scale move: combined 2023 total deposits (Capital One standalone) ranked #26 among reporting bank holding companies per Federal Reserve Y-9C data, and management framed the acquisition as necessary to compete with the nation's largest banks [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-039259#main].

The transaction closed May 18, 2025 [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2026-03-25_0001193125-26-124131#main:ITEM4]. At close, it contributed $106.9 billion of deposits — meaningfully above the $84B figure cited in the pre-close deal pitch, indicating either deposit growth at Discover between announcement and close or a difference in what was being measured (total vs. direct-to-consumer) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM7] [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-040125#main]. The packet does not reconcile these two figures.

## Distribution Network and Customer Value Proposition

Capital One's deposit-gathering model rests on a hybrid digital/physical footprint: no-fee national bank branding paired with a small physical network. As of early 2024, materials cite 259 branches, 55 Cafés in 21 of the top 25 MSAs, 16,000+ cash deposit locations, and 80,000+ fee-free ATMs [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-039259#main]. A same-day earnings-call filing instead states 250 branches, 80,000 fee-free ATMs, and 16,000 cash deposit locations [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-040125#main] — the branch count differs from the investor-deck figure filed the same day, and the packet does not explain the gap. By July 2024, a CRA/community filing cites branches in the DC, New York, and Gulf Coast metro footprints, Cafés in 21 of the top 25 MSAs, 16,000+ cash deposit locations, and "more than 70,000" fee-free ATMs [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-07-17_0001193125-24-180490#main] — a lower ATM figure than the 80,000+ cited five months earlier, again unreconciled in the packet.

The customer value proposition centers on fee elimination: no fees, no minimums, no overdraft fees, with Capital One repeatedly described as the only major bank offering free overdraft protection without minimum balance requirements [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-07-17_0001193125-24-180490#main]. Since eliminating overdraft fees in 2021, customers are stated to have saved over $500 million in potential fees [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-07-17_0001193125-24-180490#main]. The bank has ranked #1 in J.D. Power's U.S. National Banking Overall Customer Satisfaction study for four years running (2020–2023) [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-039259#main]. Stated forward commitments include growing Bank On–certified checking accounts (360 Checking) by at least 50% over the then-current base, and enabling access for roughly 100,000 ITIN-holding consumers through enhanced digital acceptance [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-07-17_0001193125-24-180490#main].

## Deposit Growth Trajectory and Mix

Reported year-end totals show steady organic growth followed by a step-change at the Discover close. Total deposits rose $14.3B to $362.7B at year-end 2024 from year-end 2023, attributed to the "national consumer banking strategy," partially offset by maturing brokered deposits (which fell to $11.6B from $18.5B) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7]. Estimated uninsured deposits were $64.9B (18% of total) at year-end 2024, essentially flat in share versus $64.2B (18%) at year-end 2023 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7].

At year-end 2025, total deposits reached $475.8B, up $113.1B from year-end 2024, "primarily driven by the Transaction and continued growth from our national banking strategy," with the Transaction alone contributing $106.9B as of the closing date [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM7]. Brokered deposits rose to $19.2B (from $11.6B), and estimated uninsured deposits rose in dollar terms to $71.9B but fell as a share of the larger base, to 15% from 18% [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM7]. Quarterly XBRL figures corroborate the timing: total deposits held near $367.5B at 2025-03-31, then jumped to $468.1B at 2025-06-30 — consistent with the May 18, 2025 close — and reached $489.1B by 2026-03-31 [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts]. The 2026 proxy statement credits 2025 performance to closing the Transaction, "on track to deliver expected deal synergies," and growth in "national digital banking franchise... checking accounts and core deposits," backed by $5.9B in marketing spend [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2026-03-25_0001193125-26-124131#main:ITEM4].

## Gaps

The packet has several limitations worth flagging rather than papering over. First, footprint figures (branches, ATMs) are inconsistent across filings within and across dates — 259 vs. 250 branches, 80,000+ vs. 70,000+ ATMs — with no source in the packet explaining the discrepancy; any brief consumer should treat these as approximate, not reconciled. Second, the $84B Discover deposit estimate cited pre-close does not match the $106.9B actually contributed at closing, and no source explains the delta. Third, the Events list for 2025–2026 consists almost entirely of 8-K filings tagged "other" with no extracted substantive content, so no deposit-specific disclosures (e.g., quarterly deposit cost/rate commentary, deposit beta, or post-merger integration deposit attrition/retention) could be drawn from them. Fourth, the packet contains no data on deposit pricing, cost of deposits, deposit mix by product (savings vs. checking vs. CDs), or competitive deposit-rate positioning — all of which would normally sit inside a "deposit strategy" brief but are simply absent from this source set.

briefs.body:
# The Discover acquisition

## Deal Structure and Mechanics

The transaction is a two-step merger executed under an Agreement and Plan of Merger dated February 19, 2024, among Discover, Capital One, and Vega Merger Sub, Inc. In the first merger, Merger Sub merges into Discover, with Discover surviving; immediately after, Discover merges into Capital One in a "second step merger," with Capital One as the surviving entity. Immediately following that, Discover Bank merges into Capital One, National Association, with Capital One, N.A. as the surviving bank [src:edgar-cof/S-4A_2025-01-03_0001193125-25-001580#main:preamble].

Consideration is 100% stock: Discover stockholders receive 1.0192 shares of Capital One common stock per Discover share (the "exchange ratio"). Based on Capital One's NYSE close on February 16, 2024 — the last trading day before announcement — that ratio represented approximately $139.86 per Discover share and aggregate merger consideration of approximately $35.3 billion. By the December 31, 2024 reference date used in the amended proxy statement, with Capital One at $178.32, the same ratio represented approximately $181.74 per Discover share [src:edgar-cof/S-4A_2025-01-03_0001193125-25-001580#main:preamble]. The deal materials characterize the exchange ratio as a 26.6% premium to Discover's share price under 100% stock consideration [src:edgar-dfs/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-039273#main]. Discover series C and series D preferred stock convert into new Capital One series O and series P preferred stock on terms "not materially less favorable"; each Discover depositary share becomes a Capital One depositary share on the same 1/100th interest basis. Outstanding Discover RSU awards convert into Capital One RSU awards, share counts adjusted by the exchange ratio [src:edgar-cof/S-4A_2024-07-26_0001193125-24-184991#main:PARTII].

Fairness-opinion work by PJT Partners produced implied exchange ratio ranges against the 1.0192x deal ratio: 0.7629x–1.1780x on a P/2024E EPS basis and 0.6723x–1.0361x on a P/TBVPS basis from comparable-company analysis [src:edgar-cof/S-4A_2025-01-03_0001193125-25-001580#main:PARTII], with a separate dividend-discount analysis producing its own implied range [src:edgar-cof/S-4_2024-04-19_0001193125-24-101304#main:PARTII] (the packet does not give the DDA range's numeric bounds).

## Strategic Rationale

Capital One frames the acquisition as advancing a "quest to build a global payments technology company," anchored in the Discover Global Network. The stated rationale is vertical integration: owning a network lets Capital One deal directly with merchants rather than through a network intermediary, capturing economics that otherwise accrue to an intermediary [src:edgar-dfs/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-040125#main]. The packet notes there are only two vertically integrated U.S.-based payments networks — American Express and Discover — competing against the larger Visa and Mastercard [src:edgar-dfs/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-040125#main]. Discover's network is described as a 40-year build: a credit card network started from scratch in the late 1980s, expanded by the 2005 PULSE acquisition (adding a national PIN debit network and roughly 4,000 member banks), and later the Diners Club acquisition for international reach [src:edgar-dfs/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-040125#main].

Scale figures cited for the combined network: 70 million merchant acceptance points across 200+ countries and territories, 1.8 million ATMs, 305 million+ global cardholders, and $550 billion+ in spend across the network [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-039259#main]. The materials also state Discover, despite this scale, remains the smallest of the four U.S.-based global payments networks, and that the acquisition adds scale and investment to make it more competitive [src:edgar-dfs/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-039259#main]. Discover CEO Michael Rhodes is quoted calling the deal an accelerant to growth that "maximizes value for our shareholders" [src:edgar-dfs/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-039259#main]. Separately, the packet notes Discover's intention (announced late 2023) to sell its student loan portfolio, with originations stopped February 1, 2024 .

## Projected Financial Metrics

Management's disclosed 2027E projections: operating expense synergy opportunity of $1.3 billion, marketing expense synergy of $0.1 billion, network synergy of $1.2 billion, adjusted EPS accretion of >15%, ROIC of 16%, and IRR of >20% (terminal value assuming 9.0x NTM P/E). Pro forma CET1 ratio at close is projected at ~14%, and 2023 pro forma insured deposits at 84% . These are management estimates tied to the assumptions stated in the filings' footnotes (non-GAAP adjusted EPS accretion, ROIC defined against Discover's synergized net income less excess capital) and should be read as projections, not realized results .

## Negotiation Timeline and Termination Terms

Discover's board first addressed inbound strategic inquiries at a September 22, 2023 meeting; a director subgroup (Maheras, Aronin, Case, Shepherd, Thierer) was formed to lead evaluation and met October 3, 2023 [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2025-02-10_0001193125-25-023100#main]. Between February 13–18, 2024, counsel exchanged merger agreement drafts: Wachtell Lipton's February 15 draft proposed a termination fee at 4.0% of transaction equity value; Sullivan & Cromwell's February 16 draft proposed 3.9%. The parties settled on $1.38 billion, ≈3.9% of the $35.3 billion aggregate merger consideration [src:edgar-dfs/425_2025-02-10_0001193125-25-023104#main]. That $1.38 billion fee is payable by either party under specified circumstances involving alternative acquisition proposals or a change in board recommendation [src:edgar-dfs/425_2024-02-22_0001193125-24-042828#main]. The agreement set a termination date 12 months after execution (i.e., February 19, 2025), automatically extendable three months (to May 19, 2025) if needed to obtain regulatory approvals [src:edgar-cof/S-4A_2025-01-03_0001193125-25-001580#main:PARTII].

## Closing Conditions and Regulatory Path

Completion requires: Discover and Capital One stockholder approvals; NYSE listing authorization for the new shares; required regulatory approvals, including the Federal Reserve Board and the OCC; effectiveness of the Form S-4; and the absence of injunctions or legal restraints [src:edgar-dfs/425_2024-02-22_0001193125-24-042828#main]. Each party's obligation is further conditioned on the other's representations and warranties being accurate, material performance of obligations, and receipt of a tax opinion that the mergers qualify as a reorganization under Internal Revenue Code Section 368(a) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM1A]. The Federal Reserve review proceeds under BHC Act Sections 3 and 4(c)(8), weighing financial and managerial resources, capital adequacy, liquidity, and management competence and integrity [src:edgar-cof/S-4_2024-04-19_0001193125-24-101304#main:PARTII]. Discover's own risk disclosures flag that regulators could impose conditions, limitations, or restrictions that delay closing, add costs, or reduce anticipated benefits, with no assurance any such conditions would be avoided [src:edgar-dfs/10-KA_2024-12-23_0001393612-24-000073#main:ITEM1A]. Capital One's 10-K separately notes it expects to incur substantial non-recurring transaction and integration expenses, which "may be greater than anticipated due to unexpected events," and flags exposure to lawsuits challenging the transaction [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM1A].

## Gaps

The packet does not establish an actual closing date, final regulatory approval terms, or shareholder vote outcomes — only the conditional framework and a termination deadline of February 19, 2025 (extendable to May 19, 2025). It contains no confirmation of whether the merger in fact closed within that window. The Events list for 2025–2026 consists of Capital One 8-Ks tagged only "other," "results," or "capital_action," several explicitly marked "Substantive Content Not Provided" — none give post-close integration status, actual (as opposed to projected) synergy realization, management/governance structure of the combined entity, or antitrust/DOJ-specific findings. No source in the packet gives the numeric range from PJT Partners' dividend discount exchange-ratio analysis, terms of the original PULSE or Diners Club acquisitions beyond the narrative summary, or details of any litigation actually filed against the transaction.

briefs.body:
# How the company makes money

## Business Model and Segments

Capital One operates as a diversified bank holding company organized into three reportable segments: Credit Card, Consumer Banking, and Commercial Banking. Credit Card covers domestic consumer and small-business card lending plus international card businesses in the United Kingdom and Canada; Consumer Banking covers deposit-gathering and lending for consumers and small businesses plus national auto lending; Commercial Banking covers lending, deposit-gathering, capital markets, and treasury management for commercial real estate and commercial/industrial customers, typically firms with annual revenues between $20 million and $2 billion [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1]. Profitability across segments is shaped by customer usage and payment patterns, expected credit losses, marketing spend, and operating efficiency; credit card purchase volume and outstandings are seasonal, peaking around the winter holidays, while credit card net charge-off rates tend to run highest in the first quarter [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1].

## Net Interest Income: The Core Revenue Engine

Net interest income — interest income (including certain fees) on loans, investment securities, and other interest-earning assets, less interest expense on deposits and wholesale borrowings — is the largest revenue component [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM7]. Credit card loans carry materially higher yields than the rest of the book: total credit card yield was 14.57% in Q1 2016 versus 6.18% for consumer banking and 3.37% for commercial banking loans in the same period [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2016-05-04_0000927628-16-000160#main:ITEM2], and the credit card yield rose to 14.67% for FY2016 and 15.21% for FY2017, versus consumer banking yields of 6.33%–6.66% and commercial banking yields of 3.47%–3.86% over the same years [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2017-02-23_0000927628-17-000115#main:ITEM7][src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7]. FY2023 net interest income growth was driven by higher average credit card loan balances and higher asset yields, partly offset by higher funding costs; period-end loans held for investment grew $8.1 billion to $320.5 billion, primarily from credit card growth, while average loans held for investment rose $19.3 billion to $311.5 billion [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM7]. Credit performance moved against the company that year: net charge-off rate rose 134 bps to 2.70%, 30+ day delinquency rose 78 bps to 3.99%, and the allowance for credit losses rose $2.1 billion to $15.3 billion (coverage ratio 4.77%) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM7]. Consolidated net interest income (XBRL) grew from $17.8 billion in FY2014 to $29.2 billion in FY2023, $31.2 billion in FY2024, and $42.9 billion in FY2025 [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts].

## Non-Interest Income: Interchange and Fees

Non-interest income "primarily consists of interchange income net of rewards expense, service charges and other customer-related fees, and other non-interest income" including mortgage representation/warranty items, securities gains/losses, and derivative gains/losses outside hedge accounting [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM7]. Net interchange fees grew steadily: $2.573 billion (FY2017), $3.179 billion (FY2019), $4.606 billion (FY2022), $4.793 billion (FY2023), $4.882 billion (FY2024) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7][src:edgar-cof/10-K_2020-02-20_0000927628-20-000102#main:ITEM7][src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7]. Service charges and other customer-related fees were $1.976 billion in FY2024, $1.667 billion in FY2023, and $1.625 billion in FY2022 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7]. Total non-interest income rose from $4.777 billion (FY2017) to $5.253 billion (FY2019), driven in FY2018 by gains on exited-business sales (including the consumer home loan portfolio) and higher purchase-volume-driven interchange [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM7][src:edgar-cof/10-K_2020-02-20_0000927628-20-000102#main:ITEM7], and continued to $7.136 billion (FY2022), $7.546 billion (FY2023), and $7.904 billion (FY2024) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7][src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts]. XBRL shows non-interest income reaching $10.556 billion in FY2025 [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts].

## Funding Sources

Deposits are described consistently across filings as "the Company's primary source of funding," providing "a stable and relatively low cost of funds," supplemented by senior/subordinated notes, securitized debt obligations, brokered deposits, FHLB advances, and repo/fed funds borrowings to maintain "a diversified mix of wholesale funding sources" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM7][src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7][src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM7][src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2017-11-01_0000927628-17-000279#main:ITEM2][src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2018-05-02_0000927628-18-000179#main:ITEM2]. As of December 31, 2023, total funding sources were $398.269 billion: deposits $348.413 billion (87%), securitized debt obligations $18.043 billion (5%), other debt $31.813 billion (8%) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM7]. Within deposits, Consumer Banking supplied $296.171 billion (74% of total, up from $270.592 billion/71% in FY2022), Commercial Banking $32.712 billion (8%, down from $40.808 billion/11%), and Other $19.530 billion (5%) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM7]. XBRL total-deposit figures show growth from $305.4 billion (2020-12-31) to $475.8 billion (2025-12-31) and $489.1 billion (2026-03-31) [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts].

## Credit Losses and Provisioning

The provision for credit losses is "driven by charge-offs, changes to allowance for loan and lease losses, and changes to unfunded lending commitments" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM7]. It was $5.9 billion (FY2018, 25.6% of NII), $7.6 billion (FY2017, 33.6%), and $6.5 billion (FY2016, 30.9%) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM7]. The allowance methodology has three components — loans collectively evaluated for impairment, an asset-specific component for individually impaired loans, and a component for purchased-credit-impaired/acquired loans with post-acquisition cash-flow declines — each supplemented for modeling and process risk [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM8][src:edgar-cof/10-K_2020-02-20_0000927628-20-000102#main:ITEM8]. A parallel expected-credit-loss allowance applies to available-for-sale securities, capped at the amount by which amortized cost exceeds fair value, with securities in unrealized-gain positions excluded [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8][src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM8].

## Segment Economics

Credit Card is the dominant profit engine. FY2021 segment data: Credit Card generated $18.880 billion revenue (62% of total) and $7.758 billion net income (63% of total); Consumer Banking $9.002 billion revenue (29%)/$3.676 billion income (30%); Commercial Banking $3.301 billion revenue (11%)/$1.532 billion income (12%); consolidated totals were $30.435 billion revenue and $12.394 billion net income [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2022-02-25_0000927628-22-000106#main:ITEM7]. FY2023 detail: Credit Card net interest income $19.729 billion, non-interest income $5.940 billion, provision $8.651 billion, net income $3.457 billion, loans held for investment $154.547 billion; Consumer Banking net income $2.258 billion, deposits $296.171 billion; Commercial Banking net income $691 million, deposits $32.712 billion; consolidated net income $4.887 billion [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM8]. Credit Card segment net income has swung with the cycle: $2.6 billion (2013), $2.5 billion (2014), $2.4 billion (2015) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM7]; $3.127 billion (2019) on $424.765 billion purchase volume and a 4.51% net charge-off rate [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2020-02-20_0000927628-20-000102#main:ITEM7]; $1.4 billion (2020), $7.8 billion (2021), $4.9 billion (2022) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM7].

## Financial Trajectory (Consolidated)

Consolidated net income per XBRL: $4.428 billion (FY2014), $3.751 billion (FY2016), $6.015 billion (FY2018), $12.390 billion (FY2021), $7.360 billion (FY2022), $4.887 billion (FY2023), $4.750 billion (FY2024), $2.453 billion (FY2025) [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts]. Non-interest expense rose from $15.056 billion (FY2020) to $30.498 billion (FY2025) [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts].

## Gaps

The packet does not explain the FY2025 jump in net interest income/expense scale (roughly $43 billion NII, $30.5 billion non-interest expense) relative to prior years — no narrative source covers what changed operationally (e.g., a major acquisition or accounting reclassification); only the raw XBRL figures are present. The 8-K event list (2025–2026) gives dates and filing types only, with no substantive content extracted, so no facts from those filings could be cited. Segment-level detail for Consumer Banking and Commercial Banking revenue drivers is thinner than for Credit Card — no packet source explains auto lending or commercial capital-markets revenue composition specifically. No packet source gives FY2024/FY2025 segment-level (vs. consolidated) profitability breakdowns.

# Marketing and brand strategy

## Strategic Framing: Brand as a Governance and Growth Lever

Capital One's proxy disclosures treat "customer advocacy and brand" as one of the fixed performance factors under the "Winning with Our Customers and Associates" pillar of executive compensation, appearing continuously across at least four proxy cycles reviewed (2016 performance factors, 2022 performance factors, 2023 performance factors, and 2025 performance factors) [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2017-03-21_0001193125-17-090802#main] [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6] [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2024-03-20_0001193125-24-072711#main:ITEM4] [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2026-03-25_0001193125-26-124131#main:ITEM4]. Net Promoter Score is the recurring proof point: the company reported record-high NPS levels in 2016 [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2017-03-21_0001193125-17-090802#main], NPS reaching "highest levels in the Company's history" in 2022 [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6], and NPS "remained high across products, channels, and experiences" in both 2023 and 2025 performance narratives [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2024-03-20_0001193125-24-072711#main:ITEM4] [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2026-03-25_0001193125-26-124131#main:ITEM4]. In 2023 the company was ranked #1 in National Bank Overall Customer Satisfaction by J.D. Power for the fourth straight year [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2024-03-20_0001193125-24-072711#main:ITEM4]. The 2016 10-K frames this as a deliberate strategy: pursuing "franchise-enhancing customer relationships" that "create and sustain significant long-term value through long and loyal customer relationships," delivered via a "brand-defining" customer experience [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM7]. The 2017 proxy echoes this with "brand-defining software applications and features" as a stated 2016 achievement [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2017-03-21_0001193125-17-090802#main]. Brand is thus positioned in the packet not as a discrete marketing-department output but as an enterprise capability tied to the technology-transformation narrative and to executive incentive design.

## Marketing Expense Trajectory and Accounting Treatment

Reported marketing expense grew from $1.561 billion in FY2014 to $5.884 billion in FY2025 [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts]. Year-by-year: FY2015 $1.744B, FY2016 $1.811B, FY2017 $1.670B, FY2018 $2.174B, FY2019 $2.274B, FY2020 $1.610B, FY2021 $2.871B, FY2022 $4.017B, FY2023 $4.009B, FY2024 $4.562B, FY2025 $5.884B [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts]. Calculated against reported noninterest expense for the same years, marketing ran roughly 12.8%–13.4% of noninterest expense in 2014–2017, dropped to about 10.7% in the pandemic-affected FY2020 ($1.610B of $15.056B), then climbed to 17.3%–21.2% from FY2021 through FY2024, and sat at 19.3% in FY2025 ($5.884B of $30.498B noninterest expense) [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts]. The FY2025 jump in both marketing spend and total noninterest expense coincides with the period in which the proxy describes "onboarding legacy Discover employees into Capital One systems" and references the "Discover Transaction" directly [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2026-03-25_0001193125-26-124131#main:ITEM4], though the packet does not itself state a closing date or attribute the expense increase explicitly to the merger. On accounting treatment, the FY2025 10-K defines marketing expense as covering "advertising (including through television, direct mail, digital, third-party partners and other channels), promotional materials and certain customer incentives, including spend-based bonuses," expensed as incurred rather than capitalized [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM8].

## Marketing Strategy Around the Discover Acquisition

Management commentary from 2024 merger-related communications gives the fullest picture of marketing intent in the packet. CEO Richard Fairbank described the deal's marketing synergy estimate as "pretty modest" — calculated as roughly 10% of the "billion dollars that Discover spends on marketing," attributed to combinable "mass customized marketing" and direct-marketing capabilities, but offset by "enhanced investment in the network and the brand of the network" [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-040125#main]. On brand positioning, Fairbank stated Discover has historically been "more of a mid-market kind of broad national focus" rather than "the very top of the market," but argued that advertising heavy-spender products still "provides lift for the whole company, because building an aspirational brand lifts all aspects of a company" [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-040125#main]. On post-close scale strategy, he framed the acquired network as a "rare unique asset" whose core constraint was scale, and positioned Capital One's card volume as the fix [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-02-20_0001193125-24-040125#main]. On spend levels, guidance in a July 2024 call pointed to roughly $2.6 billion of marketing spend in the second half of that year, attributed to both deliberate growth investment and rising competitive intensity "at the top of the market" pushing up acquisition costs; Fairbank noted the second half "virtually every year" carries more marketing spend than the first half, consistent with the prior year's pattern [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-07-24_0000927628-24-000256#main]. Separately, an April 2024 call described the pending deal as creating a "Consumer Banking and global payments platform" with "powerful brands" and a franchise "of more than 100 million customers," and addressed antitrust positioning directly, noting the combined entity would still operate alongside three other networks post-close [src:edgar-cof/425_2024-04-26_0000927628-24-000164#main].

## Competitive Threats to Brand and Marketing Effectiveness

Both the FY2025 10-K and the 10-Q covering period ending 2025-06-30 carry near-identical risk-factor language: competitors "have developed, or may develop, substantially greater financial and other resources," may offer "richer value propositions," and "may use more effective advertising, marketing or cross-selling strategies to acquire and retain more customers, capture a greater share of spending and borrowings" and secure more attractive co-brand programs [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1A] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2025-07-31_0000927628-25-000247#main:ITEM1A]. Both filings warn that customer attrition combined with rate/fee concessions to retain customers "could reduce our revenues and therefore our earnings" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1A] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2025-07-31_0000927628-25-000247#main:ITEM1A]. Post-acquisition, the 10-K adds that the Global Payment Network exposes the company to "substantial and increasingly intense competition" from both traditional payment networks and "new, emerging alternative payment providers," including direct competition for Network Partners issuing cards on the network [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1A].

## Reputation and Community Commitments Tied to Brand

The 2026 proxy discloses an "historic $265 billion Community Benefits Plan in connection with the Discover Transaction," described as "the largest acquisition-related community commitment plan in the history of the U.S. banking system" [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2026-03-25_0001193125-26-124131#main:ITEM4]. The same disclosure reports Capital One ranked #36 on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For list in 2025, its 14th consecutive year on the list [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2026-03-25_0001193125-26-124131#main:ITEM4] — down from #15 in the 2024 proxy (third consecutive year in the top 15, twelfth consecutive year overall) [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2024-03-20_0001193125-24-072711#main:ITEM4] and #10 in the 2023 proxy [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6].

## Gaps

The packet does not contain: channel-level marketing mix (digital vs. broadcast vs. direct mail spend splits), specific campaign or creative content, brand-tracking metrics such as aided/unaided awareness, segment-level marketing allocation (Domestic Card vs. Consumer Banking vs. Commercial Banking vs. network), actual realized marketing synergies post-close versus the "modest 10%" estimate, the merger closing date itself, or marketing ROI/customer-acquisition-cost data beyond qualitative statements about "competitive intensity." Fortune ranking data exists only for 2023, 2024, and 2025 proxy years within this packet — no earlier-year figure is present for direct comparison to the #10/#15/#36 trend. Any brief claims beyond these bounds would be unsupported by the corpus as provided.

# Partnership history

## Partnership history

### Portfolio acquisitions that built the co-brand book (2015–2019)

Capital One's retail partnership card business grew mainly through acquisition. On December 1, 2015, it closed the acquisition of General Electric Capital Corporation's Healthcare Financial Services business, adding roughly $9.2 billion in assets, including $8.2 billion of loans [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM1]. On September 25, 2017, it acquired credit card assets and liabilities of World's Foremost Bank — Cabela's Incorporated's bank subsidiary — from Synovus Bank, adding approximately $5.7 billion to the domestic credit card loans held-for-investment portfolio [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM1], a figure repeated in the FY2018 10-K [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM1]. On October 5, 2018, Capital One completed the Bass Pro cobrand credit card portfolio acquisition, adding approximately $534 million to the same portfolio [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM1].

### The Walmart program: contract, portfolio purchase, launch

The Walmart relationship split the card-issuance contract from the receivables purchase into two separate steps. On July 26, 2018, Capital One announced a new long-term credit card program agreement making it the exclusive issuer of Walmart's cobrand and private-label credit card program in the U.S. [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM1]. On January 22, 2019, it announced a definitive agreement to acquire the existing Walmart receivables portfolio, expected at closing to be approximately $9 billion [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2019-02-20_0000927628-19-000093#main:ITEM1]. The program launched on September 24, 2019, making Capital One the exclusive issuer of Walmart's cobrand and private-label card program [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2020-02-20_0000927628-20-000102#main:ITEM1] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1]. The portfolio acquisition closed October 11, 2019, adding approximately $8.1 billion to domestic credit card loans held for investment — below the ~$9 billion estimated at announcement [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2020-02-20_0000927628-20-000102#main:ITEM1] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1].

### Walmart card economics over time

CFPB-filed card agreements show pricing on the Walmart Rewards product moving upward across four snapshots. As of December 31, 2020: 0% introductory APR for the first 9 months, non-introductory purchase/cash-advance rates of 17.99%–26.99%, transfer APR 17.99%–26.99%, cash-advance APR 26.99%, no annual fee, 3% transfer fee, late fees up to $39 [src:cfpb-agreements/2020_Q4#ex_Capital_One_Credit_Card_Agreement_for_Capital_One_Walmart_Re]. The same filing describes a separately-detailed rewards program and promotional "Segments," including a waived-interest offer with no interest charges on purchases for a specified period [src:cfpb-agreements/2020_Q4#ex_Capital_One_Credit_Card_Agreement_for_Capital_One_Walmart_Re]. As of September 30, 2021, the flat purchase/quick-cash APR was 26.99%, same ≥25-day grace period, no annual fee, late fee up to $39 [src:cfpb-agreements/2021_Q4#ex_CAPITAL_ONE_NATIONAL_ASSOCIATION_Credit_Card_Agreement_for_W]. As of March 31, 2023, the range widened: 0% intro APR for 9 months, non-intro rates 17.99%–28.99%, transfer APR 17.99%–28.99%, cash-advance APR 28.99% [src:cfpb-agreements/2023_Q4#ex_CAPITAL_ONE_NATIONAL_ASSOCIATION_Credit_Card_Agreement_for_C]. A later filing using the same March 31, 2023 effective date lists a flat 28.99% purchase/quick-cash APR [src:cfpb-agreements/2024_Q1#ex_CAPITAL_ONE_NATIONAL_ASSOCIATION_Credit_Card_Agreement_for_W]. The product name itself shifts between "Capital One Walmart Rewards® Cards" (2020, 2023 Q4 filings) and "Walmart Rewards® Cards" (2021 Q4, 2024 Q1 filings) [src:cfpb-agreements/2020_Q4#ex_Capital_One_Credit_Card_Agreement_for_Capital_One_Walmart_Re] [src:cfpb-agreements/2023_Q4#ex_CAPITAL_ONE_NATIONAL_ASSOCIATION_Credit_Card_Agreement_for_C] [src:cfpb-agreements/2021_Q4#ex_CAPITAL_ONE_NATIONAL_ASSOCIATION_Credit_Card_Agreement_for_W] [src:cfpb-agreements/2024_Q1#ex_CAPITAL_ONE_NATIONAL_ASSOCIATION_Credit_Card_Agreement_for_W]; the packet does not explain the change.

### Partnership exits and portfolio sales (2019–2022)

Alongside acquisitions, Capital One periodically shed partnership relationships. In Q2 2019, it decided to exit "several small partnership portfolios" in Credit Card, selling approximately $900 million of receivables and transferring approximately $100 million to held-for-sale as of June 30, 2019, producing a $49 million gain on sale in other non-interest income and a $68 million allowance release [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2020-02-20_0000927628-20-000102#main:ITEM1]. The same figures recur in the Q1 and Q2 2020 10-Qs [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2020-05-01_0000927628-20-000173#main:ITEM2] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2020-08-06_0000927628-20-000242#main:ITEM2]. None of these filings name the exited partners. In Q4 2020, Capital One agreed to sell a partnership credit card loan portfolio of approximately $2.1 billion — transferred to held-for-sale as of September 30, 2020 — resulting in a $327 million allowance release [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1]; again no counterparty is named. The Q1 2022 earnings release reports a further "gain on sale of partnership card portfolios" of $192 million pre-tax, $0.35 diluted EPS impact [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2022-04-26_0000927628-22-000152#ex_ex991q12022earningsrelease.htm], with no partner identified and no portfolio size given.

## Gaps

- The packet never names the partnerships exited in Q2 2019, Q4 2020, or Q1 2022 — only aggregate dollar and P&L figures. Any claim about which retailers left the program is unsupported by this corpus.
- No source in the packet covers co-brand relationships besides Walmart, Cabela's/World's Foremost Bank, Bass Pro, and the GE Capital HFS deal. Other Capital One retail partnerships, if any, are not evidenced here.
- The Events list contains 29 Capital One 8-K filings dated August 2025 through August 2026, tagged only with category labels (other, results, capital_action) and no extracted text. None can be cited for partnership content — this is a full coverage gap for the most recent year.
- The Walmart card-agreement product-name variance ("Capital One Walmart Rewards®" vs. "Walmart Rewards®") appears across filings with no explanation in the packet.
- No source documents the current status of the Walmart exclusivity arrangement as of 2026; the latest confirmed statement in the packet dates to the FY2020 10-K [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1].
