briefs.body:
# Regulatory posture

## Enforcement History: Consent Orders and Penalties

Capital One's most significant enforcement record centers on a 2020 OCC consent order against Capital One, N.A. covering compliance risk management, data governance, capital planning, and internal controls. The order required a board-level Compliance Committee (majority independent directors) that meets quarterly and reports progress to the Examiner-in-Charge within 45 days of quarter-end, plus a Comprehensive Action Plan combining a Consent Order Action Plan and Data Governance Plan, both subject to OCC "no supervisory objection" review [src:enforcement/occ-2020-aml-consent-order-cobna#main]. It mandated root-cause analysis of internal-control failures identified by internal audit or federal regulators "since 2017," enhanced capital-planning governance, and a training program covering front-line, compliance, and audit staff [src:enforcement/occ-2020-aml-consent-order-cobna#main]. The order was issued as a cease-and-desist order under 12 U.S.C. § 1818(b), (e), (h)(2), and (i), remaining in force until amended or terminated in writing by the OCC [src:enforcement/occ-2020-aml-consent-order-cobna#main].

Separately, per Capital One's own FY2023 10-K, the company entered consent orders with the Federal Reserve and OCC in August 2020 tied to the 2019 Cybersecurity Incident, paying a civil monetary penalty under the OCC agreement; both regulators have since terminated those orders. In January 2021, Capital One, N.A. paid a separate civil monetary penalty assessed by FinCEN for AML violations alleged to have occurred between 2008 and 2014 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1A]. The packet does not specify whether the enforcement-corpus AML/BSA order is the same instrument as the FinCEN action or the terminated Fed/OCC cybersecurity orders — this is flagged below.

## Current Regulatory Priorities and Risk Framing

Across ten years of 10-K risk factors, Capital One's disclosed regulatory perimeter has both widened and sharpened in language. The FY2015 filing frames scrutiny broadly — comprehensive regulation and periodic examination by the Federal Reserve, SEC, OCC, FDIC and CFPB, with DOJ investigation exposure [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM1A]. FY2020 and FY2021 filings repeat near-identical language on formal enforcement actions and nonpublic supervisory findings restricting activities or M&A capacity [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1A] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2022-02-25_0000927628-22-000106#main:ITEM1A]. The FY2023 filing names specific priority areas — AML/sanctions, privacy/data security, service-provider use, fair lending, and technology-enabled activities — and explicitly cites the AML Act of 2020 as a driver of continued scrutiny [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1A]. FY2024 adds AI to that list and introduces regulator language on "escalating consequences for banks that do not timely resolve open issues or have repeat issues," plus unfair-or-deceptive-practices exposure [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM1A]. The FY2025 filing (filed 2026-02-19) restates these priorities and adds a standalone risk factor citing the "structure of the credit card industry" and prosecutorial focus on banks as litigation/enforcement drivers, alongside new supervisory exposure discussed below [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1A].

## Capital Regulation: Stress Capital Buffer Trajectory

Capital One's stress capital buffer (SCB) — recalibrated annually off Federal Reserve severely-adverse stress-test results, floored at 2.5% — has moved materially over the disclosed period: 2.5% for Oct 2021–Sept 2022 (min. CET1/Tier1/Total of 7.0%/8.5%/10.5%) [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2022-07-29_0000927628-22-000246#main:ITEM2]; 3.1% for Oct 2022–Sept 2023 (7.6%/9.1%/11.1%) [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2023-05-05_0000927628-23-000168#main:ITEM2] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM7]; 4.8% for Oct 2023–Sept 2024 (9.3%/10.8%/12.8%); and 5.5% for Oct 2024–Sept 2025 (10.0%/11.5%/13.5%) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7]. The 2025 stress test dropped the requirement to a final 4.5% for Oct 2025–Sept 2026 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM7]. On February 4, 2026, the Fed notified all participating firms it would hold SCB requirements at current levels pending public comment on its Stress Testing Transparency Proposal, meaning Capital One's 4.5% SCB is set to persist through September 30, 2027 absent further action [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2026-05-07_0000927628-26-000048#main:ITEM2]. The Bank entity (Capital One, N.A.) is not subject to the SCB rule; under OCC capital regulations its conservation buffer is fixed at 2.5% [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7]. Underlying this framework, reported CET1 capital grew from $28.8B (2016) to $73.0B (2025) [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts], though the packet does not connect this dollar growth to the ratio moves above (denominator/risk-weighted-asset figures are absent).

## Discover Acquisition: Inherited Regulatory Exposure

The Discover transaction imported standing regulatory matters. Discover operated under a 2020 CFPB consent order requiring a redress and compliance plan, at least $10 million in consumer redress, and a $25 million civil money penalty, plus a September 2023 FDIC consent order requiring an improved consumer compliance management system and enhanced board oversight [src:edgar-cof/S-4A_2024-07-26_0001193125-24-184991#main:PARTII]. Discover also disclosed an unresolved card-product-misclassification matter, an associated regulatory-penalty charge taken in Q2 2024, and a cooperating SEC investigation [src:edgar-cof/S-4A_2024-07-26_0001193125-24-184991#main:PARTII]. Capital One's FY2025 10-K confirms it "assumed the contingencies and liabilities of Discover," including ongoing litigation, government investigations, and enforcement actions tied to Discover's pre-Transaction conduct [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1A].

## Emerging Supervisory Matter: OCC Debanking Review

In December 2025 the OCC issued preliminary findings from a supervisory review — conducted under Executive Order 14331, "Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans" — of the nine largest OCC-regulated banks, including Capital One, N.A., examining whether those banks debanked or discriminated against customers based on political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities. The OCC states the review is ongoing [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1A]. The packet does not include the content of the preliminary findings themselves.

## Gaps

- The packet does not clarify whether the "OCC consent order 2020 (Capital One, N.A. – AML/BSA)" enforcement document is the same instrument as the August 2020 Fed/OCC cybersecurity-related consent orders described in the 10-K, or the January 2021 FinCEN AML penalty — the excerpted Articles (capital planning, internal controls, data governance) read as cybersecurity/operational-risk remediation rather than AML-specific terms, but the doc's own title says AML/BSA. This should not be resolved by inference; it needs source reconciliation.
- No dollar figures are given for the 2020 OCC civil monetary penalty, the FinCEN 2021 penalty, or any Capital One-specific penalty tied to the Discover-inherited CFPB/FDIC orders beyond Discover's own disclosed $10M/$25M figures.
- The OCC debanking review's substantive preliminary findings, and any Capital One-specific outcome, are not in the packet.
- No risk-weighted-asset figures accompany the CET1 dollar series, so capital-ratio trend cannot be independently derived from the governed observations alone.

# Segment map

## Segment Structure and Definitions

Capital One organizes continuing operations into three reportable segments — Credit Card, Consumer Banking, and Commercial Banking — plus an Other category for activity not attributable to a segment, such as the corporate investment portfolio and asset/liability management performed by the centralized Corporate Treasury group [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7]. As of the FY2025 10-K, the segments are defined as: Credit Card (domestic consumer card lending, personal loans, domestic small business card lending, and international card businesses in the U.K. and Canada); Consumer Banking (deposit gathering and lending for consumers and small businesses, national auto lending, and Global Payment Network services); and Commercial Banking (lending, deposit gathering, capital markets, and treasury management for commercial real estate and commercial/industrial customers, typically companies with $20 million to $2 billion in annual revenue) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1]. The acquired Home Loan business is reported as discontinued operations and excluded from segment results [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1]. The same filing notes structural seasonality: credit card purchase volume and receivables run highest around the winter holidays, while credit card net charge-off rates are typically highest in Q1 [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2026-02-19_0000927628-26-000024#main:ITEM1].

Within Consumer Banking, the auto loan book is monitored by FICO score at origination and the retail banking book by delinquency status — this credit-quality framing is unchanged between the Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 10-Qs [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2026-05-07_0000927628-26-000048#main:ITEM1] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2026-07-28_0000927628-26-000089#main:ITEM1].

## Reporting Methodology and Reclassifications

Segment results are reported on a continuing-operations basis and are built to approximate stand-alone business performance using internal allocation methodologies, principally funds transfer pricing (FTP) on a matched-maturity basis: business segments get a funds credit for sources of funds (e.g., deposits from Consumer and Commercial Banking) and a funds charge for use of funds, with total interest income and net fees attributed directly to the originating segment [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM8] [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7]. Capital One states it periodically revises segment definitions or allocation methodology and recasts prior periods accordingly [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7].

One documented recasting: in Q1 2019 the company changed how it allocates tax benefits on certain tax-advantaged investments within Commercial Banking, recasting prior periods. The change reduced previously reported Commercial Banking total net revenue by $26 million (three months) and $88 million (nine months) ended September 30, 2018, with an offsetting increase to Other and no consolidated impact [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2019-10-31_0000927628-19-000312#main:ITEM1]. The same recast reduced Commercial Banking revenue by $30 million for the three months ended March 31, 2018 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2019-05-01_0000927628-19-000177#main:ITEM1], and by $32 million and $62 million for the three and six months ended June 30, 2018 [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2019-07-31_0000927628-19-000274#main:ITEM1]. This followed an earlier Q1 2018 change that began including tax benefits of losses on certain tax-advantaged investments in Commercial Banking on a taxable-equivalent basis, offset in Other [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2018-05-02_0000927628-18-000179#main:ITEM1].

## Credit Card Segment Trajectory

FY2022 Credit Card results (10-K FY2022): net interest income $16,584M (+18% YoY), non-interest income $5,771M (+20%), total net revenue $22,355M (+18%), provision for credit losses $4,265M (vs. a $902M benefit in 2021), non-interest expense $11,627M (+21%), income before tax $6,463M (-36%), net income $4,927M (-36%). Average loans held for investment were $120,392M at a 16.21% average yield; net charge-offs were $3,048M (2.53% rate); purchase volume was $587,283M (+11%); period-end loans HFI reached $137,730M (+20% vs. 2021) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2023-02-24_0000927628-23-000117#main:ITEM7].

Segment-note detail for FY2019 shows Credit Card net interest income of $14,461M, non-interest income $3,888M, total net revenue $18,349M, provision $4,992M, non-interest expense $9,271M, and net income $3,127M, on loans HFI of $128,236M [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. FY2018 Credit Card figures: net interest income $14,167M, non-interest income $3,520M, total net revenue $17,687M, provision $4,984M, non-interest expense $8,542M, net income $3,191M, loans HFI $116,361M [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8].

Longer-run net income narrative: $2.6B (2013), $2.5B (2014), $2.4B (2015) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2016-02-25_0000927628-16-000140#main:ITEM7]; $2.2B (2016), $1.9B (2017) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7]. The FY2017 10-K flagged that Domestic Card charge-off pressure from loan seasoning was expected to moderate with only a small 2018 impact [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7].

## Consumer Banking Segment Trajectory

FY2024 Consumer Banking results: net interest income $8,023M (-8% YoY), non-interest income $695M (+18%), total net revenue $8,718M (-6%), provision $1,435M (+23%), non-interest expense $5,372M (+4%), net income $1,460M (-35%). Average loans HFI totaled $75,973M ($74,692M auto, $1,281M retail banking) at an 8.70% yield; average deposits were $303,873M at a 3.23% rate; net charge-offs were $1,593M (2.10% rate); auto originations were $34,542M (+28%) [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM7].

FY2019 segment-note data: net interest income $6,732M, non-interest income $643M, total net revenue $7,375M, provision $938M, non-interest expense $4,091M, net income $1,799M, loans HFI $63,065M, deposits $213,099M [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. FY2018: net interest income $6,549M, total net revenue $7,212M, provision $838M, net income $1,800M, loans HFI $59,205M, deposits $198,607M [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. Guidance in the FY2017 10-K and the Q3 2017 10-Q both anticipated a gradual increase in the auto finance charge-off rate with moderating growth [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM7] [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2017-11-01_0000927628-17-000279#main:ITEM2].

## Commercial Banking and Other Category

Commercial Banking FY2019: net interest income $1,983M, total net revenue $2,814M, provision $306M, net income $621M, loans HFI $74,508M, deposits $32,134M [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. FY2018: net interest income $2,044M, total net revenue $2,788M, provision $83M, net income $806M, loans HFI $70,333M, deposits $29,480M [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. The Q3 2017 10-Q flagged credit pressure concentrated in oil field service and taxi medallion lending [src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2017-11-01_0000927628-17-000279#main:ITEM2].

The Other category carried near-zero or negative net income in both years shown — a net loss of $14M in FY2019 and net income of $228M in FY2018 — consistent with its role as a residual for treasury/investment-portfolio activity and offsetting reclassifications rather than an operating business [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8].

## Consolidated Context

Consolidated FY2019 segment reconciliation: net interest income $23,340M, total net revenue $28,593M, provision $6,236M, net income $5,533M, loans HFI $265,809M, deposits $262,697M [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]; FY2018: net interest income $22,875M, net income $6,025M, loans HFI $245,899M, deposits $249,764M [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM8]. XBRL company-facts data extend consolidated net income and net interest income through FY2025 (net income $2,453M; net interest income $42,878M) and FY2024 (net income $4,750M; net interest income $31,208M), plus consolidated loans HFI up to 2026-03-31 ($447,754M) [src:edgar-cof/xbrl_companyfacts], but the packet contains no segment-level breakdown for FY2020–FY2025 to allocate these consolidated totals across Credit Card, Consumer Banking, and Commercial Banking.

## Recent Filing Activity

The event log lists Capital One 8-K filings from August 2025 through August 2026, nearly all tagged "(other)," with one tagged "(results)" (2026-04-21) and one "(capital_action)" (2026-04-07) [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2026-04-21_0000927628-26-000039] [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2026-04-07_0001193125-26-145764]. None of these events carry segment-level content in the packet.

## Gaps

- No segment-level financial table (revenue, provision, net income) is present for FY2020, FY2021, FY2023, or FY2025 — only FY2018, FY2019, FY2022 (Credit Card only), and FY2024 (Consumer Banking only) are covered, leaving the post-2020 Commercial Banking and Other trajectory largely undocumented.
- Commercial Banking has no FY2022+ figures in the packet, and no segment data at all exists for FY2020–FY2021, a period covering pandemic-era credit swings.
- The 8-K event list gives dates and broad categories only ("other," "results," "capital_action") with no segment-specific substance — several entries are explicitly marked "Substantive Content Not Provided."
- XBRL governed observations are consolidated-entity-only; no segment-tagged XBRL facts are in the packet, so recent-year segment allocation cannot be derived from them.
- The 30+ day delinquency rate figure for Credit Card FY2022 (3.46%) is truncated in the source table with no comparison-year value included.

briefs.body:
# The technology thesis

## The Technology Thesis

### Core Claim: Technology as Business Model, Not Utility

Capital One's own disclosures frame technology as embedded in the operating model rather than a support function. The FY2017 10-K states the company is "embedding technology, data and software development deeply into our business model and how we work," and identifies operational risk as arising directly from "faulty or disabled computer systems" and dependence on "the security, capability and continuous availability" of its technology systems [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2018-02-21_0000927628-18-000107#main:ITEM1A]. This framing — technology as a source of both competitive differentiation and operational risk — persists across every subsequent filing in the packet.

### The AWS Migration: A Decade-Long, Escalating Commitment

The packet documents a clear progression in how Capital One describes its cloud dependency. In the FY2016 10-K, the company was "in the process of migrating a number of our core systems and customer-facing applications to Amazon Web Services" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2017-02-23_0000927628-17-000115#main:ITEM1A]. By the FY2019 10-K and the 2019 10-Q, language had hardened to "migrated substantially all, and intend to migrate all, of our core information technology systems and customer-facing applications to third-party cloud infrastructure platforms, principally AWS" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2020-02-20_0000927628-20-000102#main:ITEM1A][src:edgar-cof/10-Q_2019-07-31_0000927628-19-000274#main:ITEM1A], repeated verbatim in the FY2020 10-K [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1A]. By the FY2021 10-K, the "intend to migrate all" qualifier is dropped: the company states it has "migrated substantially all aspects of our core information technology systems and customer-facing applications" to AWS [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2022-02-25_0000927628-22-000106#main:ITEM1A] — signaling the transition was treated as functionally complete. The FY2023 10-K adds new risk surface: providers who "also rely on AWS," supply-chain exposure, and scenarios where platforms "fail to scale" or exhibit "degradation in service" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2024-02-23_0000927628-24-000094#main:ITEM1A]. This is a company narrating deepening, not diversifying, its cloud concentration risk over eight years of filings, with AWS named as the principal provider in every version.

Proxy statements corroborate the milestone: the 2020 performance narrative cites having "exited all of our data centers" as part of "substantial progress on our technology transformation" [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2021-03-24_0001193125-21-092722#main:ITEM3], and the 2022 performance discussion still credits "the full exit from our data centers" and a "modern tech stack" as a source of "strategic, financial, operational, and customer benefits" [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6]. The 2023 performance narrative continues crediting "financial savings and operational benefits from 2020 exit from data centers" [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM4].

### Compensation Design: Technology Investment as an Explicit Performance Factor

Across four proxy years in the packet (2019, 2021 context, 2023, 2024), "disciplined investments in infrastructure, technology and growth initiatives" appears as a named performance factor in executive pay decisions, not incidental commentary. The 2018 performance year credits "accelerated focus on cloud capabilities, modern software engineering and delivery, and enhanced cybersecurity capabilities" [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2019-03-20_0001193125-19-080807#main:ITEM5]. The 2022 performance year credits investment in "public cloud, enterprise platforms, automation, and data and machine learning tools," alongside a 40% increase in marketing spend to $4 billion [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6]. The 2023 performance year extends this to explicit AI language: "Expanded enterprise platforms, automation capabilities, and data machine learning and artificial intelligence tools" and "$4 billion" in marketing investment [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2024-03-20_0001193125-24-072711#main:ITEM4]. Board composition reflects the same emphasis: Aparna Chennapragada, a Google product executive with AI/ML and augmented-reality experience, was added to the board in 2018, with CEO Fairbank explicitly citing her "deep understanding of the intersection of technology, information, artificial intelligence, and customer experience" [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2018-03-01_0000927628-18-000112#ex_exhibit991-pressrelease.htm][src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2019-03-20_0001193125-19-080807#main:ITEM5].

### Risk Disclosure: From Migration Execution Risk to AI-Era Competitive Risk

Risk factor language evolves in substance, not just in cloud-migration status. The FY2020 10-K flags that "adoption of new technologies, such as distributed ledger technologies, artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, can present unforeseen challenges in applying and relying on existing compliance systems" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2021-02-25_0000927628-21-000094#main:ITEM1A]. By the FY2024 10-K, AI is named as a driver of industry change directly tied to financial performance: "Our industry is subject to rapid and significant technological changes, including due to the increasing development and use of AI, and our ability to meet our customers' needs and expectations is key to our ability to grow revenue and earnings" [src:edgar-cof/10-K_2025-02-20_0000927628-25-000092#main:ITEM1A]. The 2022 proxy also notes that "the OCC formally closed Capital One's cyber-related consent order" after "sustained investment and focus" on risk and control [src:edgar-cof/DEF14A_2023-03-22_0001193125-23-076700#main:ITEM6], tying technology investment directly to regulatory relief.

### The Brex Acquisition: The Thesis Made Explicit

The clearest statement of intent in the packet is the January 2026 announcement of Capital One's agreement to acquire Brex for $5.15 billion in stock and cash [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2026-01-22_0001193125-26-019543#ex_d97758dex991.htm]. Brex is described as "a modern, AI-native software platform" that "leverages AI agents to help customers automate complex workflows," and Fairbank frames the deal as accelerating a founding ambition to "build a payments company at the frontier of the technology revolution" [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2026-01-22_0001193125-26-019543#ex_d97758dex991.htm]. This positions the AWS-and-data-center narrative of 2016–2024 as infrastructure groundwork for a subsequent acquisition strategy centered on AI-native platforms, with the deal expected to close mid-2026 [src:edgar-cof/8-K_2026-01-22_0001193125-26-019543#ex_d97758dex991.htm].

## Gaps

- The packet contains no dollar figures for total technology or cloud capital expenditure in any year — only qualitative characterizations ("disciplined investments," "significant... investments"). Any capex trend claim is unsupported.
- No packet source states what percentage of workloads or systems remained non-AWS at any point; "substantially all" and "primarily all" are the only granularity available.
- The Brex deal's strategic rationale is sourced only to the announcement press release; no post-signing integration, regulatory approval, or synergy-target documents are in the packet.
- The events list for 2025–2026 (multiple 8-Ks) is present only as filing metadata with no extracted content in this packet — their relevance to the technology thesis cannot be assessed.
- No source directly quantifies AI/ML deployment scale (e.g., number of models, customer-facing AI features) beyond the general references to "data machine learning and artificial intelligence tools."
